 Transfer Pricing Compliance in India: Key Filing Requirements for 30 November 2026
 17 November 2026 
 Posted by India Briefing 
 Written by 
 Archana Rao 
 In this article 
 Businesses operating in India with international related-party transactions must review their outstanding transfer pricing compliance obligations ahead of the 30 November 2026 deadline for Assessment Year (AY) 2026-27. The deadline covers the filing of income tax returns for applicable taxpayers, along with specific transfer pricing reporting requirements, including the Master File and safe harbour forms.

 Transfer Pricing Compliance Requirements by 30 November 
 Compliance requirement 
 Applicable provision / form 
 Applicability 
 Income tax return filing
 Section 139(1) – Applicable ITR form
 Taxpayers required to furnish an accountant’s report under Section 92E
 Master File – Part A
 Section 92D(4); Rule 10DA; Form 3CEAA
 All constituent entities of an international group
 Master File – Part B

 Source: Income Tax Act, IT Department ; Ministry of Finance, GoI
 India’s transfer pricing regulations require businesses to ensure that transactions between associated enterprises (AEs) comply with the arm’s length principle.
 For FY 2025-26 (or AY 2026-27), compliance continues under the Income Tax Act 1961, even though the Income Tax Act 2025 came into effect on 1 April 2026. Businesses should therefore complete their remaining obligations under the existing transfer pricing framework.
 Income tax return filing for AY 2026-27
 Companies subject to transfer pricing provisions must ensure that their income tax returns are filed within the applicable statutory timeline.
 For taxpayers required to furnish an accountant’s report under Section 92E of the Income Tax Act 1961, the applicable ITR filing deadline for AY 2026-27 is 30 November.
 The return should be consistent with the company’s audited financial statements, related-party disclosures and transfer pricing documentation.

 Master file submission
 Indian constituent entities of multinational enterprise (MNE) groups may be required to furnish a master file under Section 92D(4) and Rule 10DA of the Income Tax Rules 1962.
 The Master File provides tax authorities with an overview of the international group’s global operations, organisational structure, business activities, value chains, intangible assets, financing arrangements and transfer pricing policies.
 Such filing requirements are divided into two parts.
 1. Part A: Applicable to constituent entities of an international group, irrespective of whether they meet the prescribed thresholds for Part B.
 2. Part B: Required where the international group satisfies both of the following conditions:
 Consolidated group revenue exceeds INR 5 billion during the accounting year
 The aggregate value of international transactions exceeds INR 500 million, or transactions involving the purchase, sale, transfer, lease or use of intangible property exceed INR 100 million
 Indian subsidiaries should coordinate with their overseas parent companies to obtain the required group-level information. It must also ensure that the Master File is consistent with the transfer pricing documentation maintained in other jurisdictions.
 Safe harbour election
 Businesses undertaking eligible international transactions may consider the safe harbour provisions under Section 92CB and Rules 10TA-10TG of the Income Tax Rules 1962.
 The framework allows eligible taxpayers to adopt prescribed transfer pricing margins or prices for specified transactions, subject to applicable conditions. This can provide greater certainty over arm’s length pricing and reduce the risk of transfer pricing disputes.
 Following the Finance Act 2025 amendments, the prescribed eligibility ceiling was increased to INR 3 billion from INR 2 billion for covered transactions.
 Eligible categories include the following:
 Software development and IT-enabled services
 Knowledge process outsourcing
 Contract research and development
 Specified intra-group loans
 Corporate guarantees
 Specified automobile-related transactions
 Businesses opting for the safe harbour framework must assess their eligibility, verify the applicable margins and comply with the prescribed reporting requirements.
 Transfer pricing documentation businesses should maintain
 Corporations must maintain appropriate documentation to substantiate the arm’s length nature of their international and specified domestic transactions. Under Section 92D and Rule 10D of the Income Tax Rules 1962, prescribed documentation should generally include the following information:
 Details of the international group and associated enterprises
 Nature, terms and value of international transactions
 Functions performed, assets employed and risks assumed (FAR analysis)
 Selection of the most appropriate transfer pricing method
 Identification of the tested party and relevant profit level indicator
 Comparable company or transaction analysis
 Benchmarking calculations and supporting financial information
 Intercompany agreements, invoices and cost-allocation workings
 The detailed documentation requirements apply where the aggregate value of international transactions exceeds INR 10 million. However, businesses below this threshold must also be able to substantiate that their transactions comply with the arm’s length principle.

 Penalties for transfer pricing non-compliance
 Failure to comply with India’s transfer pricing documentation and reporting requirements can result in financial penalties and additional tax adjustments.
 Provision 
 Nature of default 
 Penalty 
 Section 271AA
 Failure to maintain or report prescribed transfer pricing information or furnishing inaccurate information
 2 per cent of the value of each relevant international or specified domestic transaction
 Section 271BA
 Failure to furnish the accountant’s report in Form 3CEB
 INR 100,000
 Section 271G
 Failure to furnish information or documents requested under Section 92D(3)
 2 per cent of the value of the relevant transaction
 Section 271GB
 Non-compliance with Country-by-Country Reporting requirements
 Prescribed fixed and continuing penalties, depending on the nature of the default
 Section 270A
 Under-reporting or misreporting of income
 50 per cent or 200 per cent of the tax payable on under-reported income, as applicable
 Transfer pricing adjustments can also affect deductions claimed by businesses operating under tax incentive provisions. For example, Section 92C(4) restricts deductions under Section 10AA and Chapter VI-A in respect of income enhanced through transfer pricing adjustments.
 Business compliance checklist
 Businesses should complete the following checks ahead of the filing deadline:
 Confirm the applicable income tax return filing requirements for AY 2026-27
 Determine whether the Indian entity is required to submit Part A or Part B of Form 3CEAA
 Coordinate with the overseas parent company to obtain the information required for master file reporting
 Evaluate eligibility for safe harbour provisions and complete Form 3CEFA, where applicable
 Reconcile transfer pricing disclosures with audited financial statements and related-party schedules
 Ensure that supporting agreements, benchmarking studies, invoices and cost-allocation records are complete and readily accessible
 Review the consistency of transfer pricing disclosures across the income tax return, Form 3CEB and Master File
 Verify that all applicable transfer pricing reporting and documentation requirements have been met

 Preparing for the 30 November transfer pricing deadline
 The 30 November 2026 deadline is an important compliance milestone for businesses subject to India’s transfer pricing framework. Companies should prioritise applicable Master File submissions, safe harbour reporting and income tax return filings while ensuring that their transfer pricing positions are supported by appropriate documentation.
 Coordination between Indian finance teams, tax advisors and overseas group entities is particularly important for multinational businesses that rely on group-level information to complete their reporting obligations. Reviewing outstanding filings, validating related-party disclosures and ensuring documentation consistency can help businesses minimise compliance gaps and reduce the risk of transfer pricing disputes.
 A well-executed audit in India is crucial to ensure compliance with local regulations, verify financial accuracy, and identify risks, while a clean, structured audit process helps businesses stay ahead and gain clear visibility into operations.
